results.title: Google Stitch Loop: An Always-On Agent for Live Products
results.content:
1. 01 It watches what you connectA repository supplies the implementation. Logs, behavior data, feedback and product documents can help explain what users experience.
2. 02 It proposes a direction before writing the fixSuggestions cite evidence. Once you choose a solution, Loop writes code in an isolated cloud sandbox and opens a GitHub pull request.
3. 03 The measurement still needs an ownerA change in traffic mix alone can cause a 12-point checkout decline. Define the denominator, the segments and the outcome before choosing a fix.
4. 04 Access starts with a global waitlistAnyone can join the list. Eligible Google AI Ultra users receive priority. Google’s launch gives no general-release date or per-loop price.

## 01 — InputsGive the agent a question it can answer [...] A checkout dashboard goes from 87% completion to 75%. Someone needs to find out whether the page broke, a campaign brought in different customers, or the analytics changed. Google Stitch Loop can take that question to a connected codebase, suggest an explanation and prepare a fix. The most valuable response may be to leave the code alone.

In its November 18 launch, Google Labs describes a long-running product agent for software that already has users. You give it a standing objective, connect GitHub and supply the evidence it needs. Two decisions stay with the team. Someone chooses which proposed solution is worth building, and someone reviews the resulting pull request before it merges. As of November 19, Google is accepting waitlist registrations.Google Labs’ Stitch Loop announcement [...] Choosing a direction starts the build. Google says Loop writes code in an isolated cloud sandbox and submits a GitHub pull request for approval. Where they help explain the work, the request includes screenshots or video. A screenshot might show that an error is legible on a phone. A reviewer still needs to confirm that an actual user can recover from the error and finish the transaction.

After a change reaches users, Loop can follow positive and negative results in the connected data. It continues watching even after the objective is met. For this to be informative, give the system a way to associate a measurement with the version a visitor saw. A pull request that merged on Monday but reached only internal testers until Thursday has two very different dates attached to it.

results.content:
# Google Stitch Loop: Always-On Agent Rewrites Code 24/7

Google Labs officially launched Stitch Loop on November 18, 2026, introducing a continuous agent that connects directly to codebases and live product metrics to identify issues, propose fixes, and write code around the clock. Unlike traditional development tools that complete a task and terminate, Stitch Loop operates indefinitely, monitoring deployed software to prevent performance regressions even after initial objectives are met.

## How Stitch Loop Works [...] Each cycle operates independently, allowing the agent to work on multiple optimization paths simultaneously. When Stitch Loop detects a metric decline or identifies a potential improvement, it generates a code proposal complete with context about the issue and expected impact. The agent then monitors whether the proposed change achieves the desired outcome, creating a feedback loop that informs future suggestions.

## Human Review Requirements [...] ## Integration With Antigravity

Stitch Loop functions as a service layer for Google's Antigravity platform, accessible through the Stitch CLI, MCP protocol, and Slack @-mentions. This architecture allows development teams to trigger optimization cycles from multiple interfaces without switching tools. The integration with Antigravity positions Stitch Loop as part of Google's broader developer tooling ecosystem rather than a standalone product.

Teams can configure Stitch Loop to monitor specific repositories, set priority metrics, and define thresholds that trigger new optimization cycles. The agent operates asynchronously, queuing suggestions and updates that developers can review during normal workflow rather than demanding immediate attention.

Coding agents let you build and ship new features fast, but their job ends the moment your pull request merges. Once code hits production, the real work starts: patching vulnerabilities, speeding up checkout, and diagnosing signup drop-offs buried in noisy feedback. For lean teams, balancing post-launch maintenance with continuous improvement is a constant challenge, yet it’s also what drives some of the world’s most successful products.

Today, we are introducing Stitch Loop, a long-running product agent from Google Labs that connects to your codebase and live metrics, finds what needs fixing, and keeps working 24/7 on your product until your goals are met. [...] Justin Toupin
